questions.stem: Which OSHA form is the annual summary of work-related injuries and illnesses?
options: OSHA 300
OSHA 301
OSHA 301A
OSHA 300A
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA 300A summarizes the establishment annual recordkeeping data and is certified and posted as required.
incorrectOptionExplanations: OSHA 300 is the log of recordable cases.
OSHA 301 is the individual incident report.
OSHA does not designate the annual summary as 301A.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 3, OSHA forms, pp. 50-51; 29 CFR 1904.29 and 1904.32

questions.stem: How quickly must a recordable case generally be entered on the OSHA 300 Log and 301 Incident Report after the employer receives the information?
options: Within 7 calendar days
Within 24 hours
Within 15 working days
By the end of the following year
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: 29 CFR 1904.29 requires entry of each recordable injury or illness within seven calendar days of receiving information that it occurred.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Twenty-four hours applies to reporting certain severe events to OSHA, not all log entries.
Fifteen working days is associated with contesting citations.
Waiting until the next year exceeds the recording requirement.

questions.stem: A remote employee trips over a file box supplied for the assigned work and receives medical treatment beyond first aid. How is work-relatedness evaluated?
options: It is automatically non-work-related because the event occurred inside the employee home
It may be work-related because the supplied file box was part of performing assigned work
It is automatically work-related because it occurred during the employee scheduled working hours
It is excluded because OSHA recordkeeping does not apply to employees working remotely
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Home cases are evaluated based on whether they are directly related to work performance rather than general home conditions.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Location at home does not automatically remove work-relatedness.
Scheduled time alone does not establish the cause or relationship to work.
Covered remote employees are not categorically excluded.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 3, work-relatedness for home injuries, pp. 45-46; 29 CFR 1904.5

questions.stem: A work-related injury requires prescription medication. What is the general recordkeeping result?
options: Do not record because the employee returned the same day
Record only if hospitalization occurred
Record the case because it involved medical treatment beyond first aid
Do not record if the employee prefers privacy
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A work-related new case is generally recordable when it results in medical treatment beyond first aid or another listed criterion.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Return to work does not remove other recording criteria.
Hospitalization is not the only recordable outcome.
Privacy rules affect how certain cases are listed, not whether a qualifying case is recorded.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 3, determining recordability, pp. 46-47; 29 CFR 1904.7

questions.stem: Which reporting time pair is correct under federal OSHA for covered work-related events?
options: All events within 7 calendar days
Fatality within 24 hours and hospitalization within 8 hours
Only fatalities must be reported
Fatality within 8 hours; in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Federal OSHA requires reporting a work-related fatality within 8 hours and specified severe nonfatal events within 24 hours.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Seven days is the general log-entry period, not the severe-event notification period.
The reporting intervals are reversed.
OSHA also requires timely reporting of specified nonfatal severe events.

questions.stem: A recordable needlestick involves another person blood. How should the employee name be handled on the OSHA 300 Log?
options: Enter a privacy case on the log and keep the employee identity on a confidential list
Record the employee name and attach the complete medical record to the publicly posted summary
Omit the event from the log because needlesticks involving blood are confidential medical matters
Record the supervisor name in place of the employee so the case remains visible without disclosure
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Specified privacy cases are entered without the employee name, while the employer maintains a confidential key for required updating and access.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Recordkeeping access does not authorize unnecessary disclosure of confidential medical information.
A qualifying privacy case remains recordable.
Substituting another person name creates an inaccurate record.

questions.stem: When is the OSHA 300A annual summary generally posted?
options: Only on the day of an OSHA inspection
From February 1 through April 30 of the following year
From January 1 through January 7
For five years continuously on the bulletin board
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The certified annual summary is posted in a conspicuous place from February 1 through April 30.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Posting is a scheduled annual requirement, not inspection-dependent.
This is not the required posting period.
Records are retained for five years, but the summary is not posted continuously for that entire period.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 3, annual summary, p. 51; 29 CFR 1904.32

questions.stem: A recorded restricted-work case later becomes a days-away case during the five-year retention period. What should the employer do?
options: Never update a prior-year log
Create a second duplicate case
Update the OSHA 300 Log to reflect the changed classification
Change the certified 300A summary only
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA records are retained for five years, and the log is updated when recorded cases change status or new information becomes available.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The log must be updated during the retention period for changes in case classification or outcome.
One incident should not be counted as two cases.
The prior annual summary is not required to be updated in the same way as the log.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 3, retention and updating, p. 53; 29 CFR 1904.33

questions.stem: A host employer provides day-to-day supervision to a temporary worker who has a recordable injury. Who generally records the case?
options: Both employers must record the same case
Neither employer because the worker is temporary
The staffing agency regardless of supervision
The host employer that provides day-to-day supervision
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The host and staffing agency should coordinate so the employer providing day-to-day supervision records the case once.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The case should be recorded once, not duplicated.
Temporary status does not remove recordkeeping coverage.
Responsibility follows day-to-day supervision for these workers.

questions.stem: A facility had 6 OSHA-recordable cases and 480,000 hours worked. What is the total case incident rate?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: TCIR = 6 x 200,000 / 480,000 = 2.5 cases per 100 full-time-equivalent workers.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides hours by cases and scales incorrectly.
This uses 480,000/60,000 rather than the incident-rate formula.
This moves the decimal one place too far.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
